name: Babur
info: Babur (1483-1530), born Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad, was a Timurid prince of Fergana who lost his Central Asian lands, ruled Kabul and in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire in northern India; he is also remembered for his memoir, the Baburnama.

facts.born: 14 February 1483 in Andijan, Fergana Valley; eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza II, descended from Timur through his father and from Genghis Khan through his mother
facts.died: 26 December 1530 in Agra; first buried at Chauburji, Agra, later reburied in Bagh-e Babur, Kabul
facts.role: Ruler of Fergana from 1494; ruler of Kabul from 1504; Padshah among the Timurids; founder and first emperor of the Mughal Empire, 1526-1530
facts.known: First Battle of Panipat; Battle of Khanwa; founding the Mughal Empire; the Baburnama; Chagatai Turkic poetry; introducing the charbagh garden to northern India

t: Babur spent his youth winning and losing Fergana and Samarkand to rival Timurids and the Uzbek Muhammad Shaybani before making Kabul his base in 1504.
Using field artillery and linked carts in the Ottoman fashion, he defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 and Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527, founding the Mughal Empire.

His memoir, the Baburnama, frank about his own faults, records his campaigns, gardens and the violence of his conquests, and is regarded as one of the earliest true autobiographies in Islamic literature.
dyk: Before the Battle of Khanwa, Babur publicly renounced wine and had his gold and silver drinking vessels broken up and the fragments given to the poor.
ev: Babur becomes Timurid ruler of Fergana on the death of his father, aged eleven
He takes Samarkand after a seven-month siege, then holds it for only 100 days
He crosses the Hindu Kush and captures Kabul, which he rules until 1526
With the help of Shah Ismail I he takes Samarkand for the third time, losing it again in 1512
He defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat and occupies Delhi and Agra
He defeats Rana Sanga of Mewar at the Battle of Khanwa
His victory at the Battle of Ghaghra ends organised Afghan resistance
Babur dies at Agra and is succeeded by his son Humayun

sections.early:
Babur was born Zahīr ud-Dīn Muhammad on 14 February 1483 in Andijan, in the Fergana Valley of present-day Uzbekistan. He was the eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza II, the Timurid ruler of Fergana and a great-great-great-grandson of Timur, and of Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, daughter of Yunus Khan, the ruler of Moghulistan and a descendant of Genghis Khan. His names were chosen by the Sufi saint Khwaja Ahrar, his father's spiritual master; the nickname Babur, generally taken from the Persian word for tiger or panther, may have spread because his Turco-Mongol soldiers found his given name hard to pronounce.

His family belonged to the Turkic Barlas tribe, of Mongol origin, which had converted to Islam centuries earlier and taken up the Turco-Persian tradition. His first language was Chagatai Turkic, and he was equally fluent in Classical Persian, the language of the Timurid elite. The lands around Fergana were held by relatives descended from Timur or Genghis Khan who were constantly at war, and rival princes fought over Samarkand to the west. The main source for his life is his own memoir, the Baburnama.
sections.rise:
In 1494, aged eleven, Babur succeeded his father, who died when a dovecote collapsed into a ravine. Two hostile uncles and nobles who favoured his younger brother Jahangir threatened him, and he kept the throne mainly through his grandmother Aisan Daulat Begum. In 1497 he took Samarkand after a seven-month siege, but a revolt at home cost him Fergana, and he held Samarkand only 100 days. In 1500-1501 he took it again, was besieged by Muhammad Shaybani, Khan of the Uzbeks, and had to give his sister Khanzada to Shaybani in marriage to leave in safety. By 1502 he had lost Fergana too and wandered the mountains, writing of the poverty and humiliation he endured in Tashkent.

In October 1504 he crossed the Hindu Kush and took Kabul from the Arghun chieftains. After a stay at Herat, where he came to know the work of the poet Mir Ali Shir Nava'i, he took the title of Padshah among the Timurids. When Shah Ismail I of Safavid Persia killed Shaybani in 1510, Babur accepted Safavid suzerainty in return for help and took Samarkand for the third time in 1511, losing it to the Uzbeks in 1512. He then trained his army, took Bajaur in 1519, Badakhshan in 1521 and Kandahar in 1522.
sections.deeds:
Turning to India, Babur claimed the Punjab as the legacy of Timur and received invitations from Daulat Khan Lodi, Governor of Punjab, and from Ala-ud-Din, uncle of the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi. On 21 April 1526, at Panipat, he met Ibrahim's army of about 100,000 soldiers and 1,000 elephants. He lashed together some 700 carts in the Ottoman fashion, placed matchlock-men and field guns behind them under the Ottoman gunners Ustad Ali Quli and Mustafa Rumi, and encircled the enemy. Ibrahim Lodi died in the battle, ending the Lodi dynasty, and Babur occupied Delhi, Gwalior and Agra.

On 16 March 1527 he defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar and his coalition of Rajput and Afghan chiefs at Khanwa, one of the first battles in India to feature cannons and muskets; K. V. Krishna Rao credits his "superior generalship". He took Chanderi in January 1528 and in May 1529 defeated the Afghan and Bengal coalition at the Ghaghra. He kept Agra as his capital, gave the conquered districts to his commanders as revenue assignments and left the zamindars and much of the Lodi fiscal system in place. He gave away the treasure he took, and his daughter Gulbadan Begum recalled that every person in Kabul received a silver coin.
sections.opponents:
Babur's rivals were first his own kin and the Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani, who repeatedly drove him from Samarkand; in India they were Ibrahim Lodi, Rana Sanga, who regarded him as a foreigner ruling in India, Medini Rai of Malwa and the Afghan Lodi loyalists. When Daulat Khan Lodi's forces were routed at Lahore in 1524, Babur burned the city for two days. Before Khanwa he denounced Rana Sanga as a kafir, proclaimed the fight a jihad and afterwards took the title of ghazi. At Chanderi in 1528 the defenders' women and children immolated themselves in a jauhar, and Babur wrote no word of admiration for his enemy.

According to the Baburnama, his campaign in northwest India targeted Hindus and Sikhs as well as apostates, an immense number were killed, and his camps built "towers of skulls of the infidels". Guru Nanak witnessed this violence and commented on it in four hymns, and historians suggest the violence of the early Mughal period contributed to Sikhism's turn from pacifism to militancy for self-defence. In modern India many Hindu nationalists target Babur as the reputed builder of the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya, accusing him of demolishing a temple for it; in 2019 the Indian Supreme Court held that nothing proves the earlier structure was demolished to build the mosque.
sections.last:
In his last months Babur was preoccupied with the succession. When his eldest son and heir Humayun fell dangerously ill at Sambhal in 1530, Babur, by a celebrated account preserved by Gulbadan Begum, walked three times round the sick-bed and prayed that the illness pass to him. Humayun recovered and Babur's health declined soon afterwards. In a secret will of 1529 he advised Humayun to administer justice according to the ways of every religion, to avoid the sacrifice of the cow, not to ruin the temples of any law-obeying community and to overlook the quarrels of Shias and Sunnis. He divided his lands between Humayun and Kamran in roughly a six-to-five ratio and urged Humayun to deal gently with his brothers.

Babur died in Agra on 26 December 1530, aged 47, and Humayun succeeded him. He was first buried at Chauburji in Agra; as he had wished, his remains were later moved to Kabul and reburied in Bagh-e Babur sometime between 1539 and 1544. The realm he left reached from the Oxus and Kabul across the Punjab and the Gangetic plain to the frontiers of Bengal and Bihar, but it remained a loose military conquest; as Asher writes, Humayun inherited "a shaky and as yet unconsolidated empire".
sections.legacy:
Babur's lasting contribution in India was military: field artillery and mobile gunpowder tactics taken from the Ottomans and from Central Asian warfare. He introduced the symmetrical four-part charbagh garden to the plains of northern India, which became an enduring trademark of Mughal architecture. F. Lehmann in the Encyclopaedia Iranica holds him largely responsible for the spread of Persian cultural influence in the subcontinent through his descendants, the Mughals.

The Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic and translated into Persian for Akbar's library by Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan in 1589, is regarded as one of the earliest true autobiographies in Islamic literature; Henry Beveridge ranked it with the confessions of Augustine and Rousseau, and Stephen Dale describes its author as "relentlessly ambitious, humorous, casually violent" and "highly cultured". Mirza Haidar ranked Babur a Turki poet "second only to Mir Ali Shir". Soviet and Uzbek sources regard him as an ethnic Uzbek, an anachronism; he is a national hero in Uzbekistan, where many of his poems became folk songs, and some sources say in Kyrgyzstan too. Pakistan named its Babur Cruise Missile after him in 2005, while in India the Babri Masjid, demolished in December 1992 amid rioting that killed more than a thousand people, keeps his name at the centre of political dispute.

summary: Babur, a Timurid prince who lost Fergana and Samarkand to his rivals, made Kabul his kingdom in 1504 and in 1526-1529 conquered northern India with artillery and field tactics learned from the Ottomans, founding the Mughal Empire. His campaigns were violent, as his own memoir records, and he left Humayun an unconsolidated realm, but also the Baburnama, his poetry and the charbagh garden.
